title: Area VI review: Flight by Reference to Instruments
intro: These questions mix the eight Tasks of Area VI, taught by instruments with full panel and partial panel as the PTS asks. Task H, recovery from unusual attitudes, gets a few more questions because the evaluator must always select it. Most join two Tasks in one hood lesson the way your learner will meet them: a level-off that ends off altitude and airspeed, a speed change in a turn that ends nose-high, an abrupt level-off that becomes a dive, a timed turn after a vacuum failure, a compass turn flown too steeply, a steep turn followed by a precession check, and a constant rate descent in a turn.

questions.q: After leveling off from a descent, your learner sets the power a little above cruise. A minute later she is 60 feet above the assigned altitude and 8 knots faster than cruise. What correction do you coach?
options: Pitch alone: lower the nose about a half bar width, since altitude can be traded for airspeed
Power alone: bring the throttle back to the cruise setting and hold the attitude while both settle
Pitch and power: lower the nose about a half bar width and take off a little power, then trim
Pitch and power, with an initial full bar width nose-down because the error is over 50 feet
questions.why: When altitude and airspeed are both high, or both low, a change in both pitch and power is needed; pitch alone works only when one is high and the other low [[23:169|IFH 7-8]] [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. Lowering the nose alone here would trade the extra altitude for still more airspeed. For an error under 100 feet the rule of thumb is a half bar width; the initial full bar width is for errors over 100 feet [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Then trim, so the airplane holds the new attitude with the controls released [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

questions.q: Your learner recovers well from a nose-high unusual attitude and is straight and level, 200 feet above the altitude you assigned. She lowers the nose to go back, and the VSI shows 900 fpm down. What do you teach?
options: The VSI is primary for pitch on the way back; aim for about 400 fpm, because 900 is overcontrolling
That is fine: after an unusual attitude she should go back at the best rate the airplane allows
She should stay at this altitude, since the IFH recovery is complete once she is straight and level
The altimeter stays primary for pitch, so she holds 900 fpm until the needle nears the altitude
questions.why: After stabilizing in straight-and-level flight, the pilot returns to the altitude the instructor or ATC assigned [[23:189|IFH 7-28]], so staying high is wrong. When returning to an altitude the VSI is the primary pitch instrument, and the rule of thumb is a rate about double the error [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]. The glass section uses this very case: 200 feet off calls for about 400 fpm, and a rate more than 200 fpm past that is overcontrolling [[23:198|IFH 7-37]]. So 900 fpm is not a good fast return; it is the overcontrolling the IFH warns about.

questions.q: Flying as your learner, the examiner levels out of a turn with the throttle friction loose, and the power creeps back. The airspeed drops 10 knots while the altitude holds. He lowers the nose, loses 100 feet, and the airspeed is still low. What do you say?
options: Good instinct: low airspeed means a nose-high attitude, so lowering the nose was right, just too much
Fixation on the airspeed: in level flight he should ignore the airspeed and hold the altitude only
A trim error: he should trim nose-down so the airplane holds cruise speed by itself, then climb back
Insufficient cross-check: low power, not a high nose, slowed him; reset power and friction, climb back
questions.why: The IFH describes this pitch error: the airspeed is low, the pilot believes the nose is high and pushes forward without noting that a low power setting caused it; the fix is a faster cross-check of all the relevant instruments before any control input [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. If the airspeed is off, check the altimeter before deciding on a power change [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]; here the altitude was holding, so power was the problem. Improper throttle friction is a listed cause of erratic power control [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Trim relieves pressures already held; it is not a substitute for the controls [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

questions.q: Using this figure, your learner, who flies a 100-knot trainer, and her friend, who flies a 200-knot single, both say they use 30° of bank for instrument turns. What do you tell them?
options: Both fly standard rate: the left panel shows that 30° gives about 3° per second at any speed
In the trainer 30° is steep, about 6.5° per second; at 200 knots it is near standard rate
In the trainer 30° is near standard rate, but at 200 knots it is steep, about 6.5° per second
Neither is steep: a turn becomes steep only past 45°, where the overbanking tendency starts
questions.why: In Figure 4-15 a constant 30° bank gives about 6.5° per second at 100 knots but about 3.2° per second at 200 knots: at the same bank, more speed means a slower rate of turn [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], so the answer that makes the trainer's turn standard rate and the fast single's turn steep has it backward. The IFH rule of thumb puts the standard-rate bank at 15 percent of the true airspeed, so 200 knots needs about 30° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. For instrument training any turn greater than standard rate is steep, and the exact bank at which a turn becomes steep is unimportant [[23:183|IFH 7-22]], so no fixed bank such as 45° defines it.

questions.q: Gyros covered, your learner is steady on 305 by the compass, and you ask for a standard-rate turn to 110 without giving a direction. She starts a left turn and plans to time it for 65 seconds. What do you teach?
options: Fine as planned: from 305 a left turn is the shorter way to any heading below 180
Turn right and time 110 seconds, because partial panel timed turns use half standard rate
Turn left as planned, but add the roll-in and roll-out time to the 65 seconds
Turn right, the shorter way: 110 is 165° away, so time it for 55 seconds
questions.why: Unless there is a reason to go the long way, turn the shortest way. The IFH shortcut: 305 minus 200 plus 20 gives a reciprocal of 125, so a turn to 110 goes right [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Divide the heading change by 3 for the seconds at standard rate [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]: 165° takes 55 seconds, while 65 seconds is the 195° turn to the left. Half standard rate is for small heading changes, and if the roll-in and roll-out rates are the same, the entry and recovery time need not be counted [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

questions.q: Under the hood your learner holds a left standard-rate turn for two full circles, then rolls out on heading. She says she now feels a right turn and starts to roll left, though the attitude indicator and turn coordinator show wings level. What is happening, and what do you teach?
options: After the long turn her inner ear now signals a turn the other way; she holds wings level by the panel
The attitude gyro precessed during the long turn, so she is right to trust the feeling until the gyro settles
A Coriolis illusion from moving her head; she should tilt her head back toward the turn to cancel the feeling
The leans from a fast roll-out; she should roll back left slowly so that her inner ear can follow the change
questions.why: In a prolonged constant-rate turn the fluid in the ear canal catches up with the canal walls and the turn is no longer felt. On the return to straight-and-level flight the fluid moves briefly the other way, which feels like a turn in the opposite direction, and a pilot who reenters the turn can lose control [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]; the same sequence leads into the graveyard spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Recovering by sensations other than sight is a listed error: trust the instruments [[23:190|IFH 7-29]]. The leans come from a bank entered too slowly to sense, and rolling back into the original bank is the very error the IFH warns about [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

questions.q: Your learner flies a left climbing turn at standard rate, 90 knots true and about 13.5° of bank. At her altitude she levels off to accelerate to her 130-knot true cruise while still turning. What do you teach about power and bank?
options: Pull power to cruise as the nose comes down, and hold 13.5°, since standard rate keeps the same bank
Keep climb power until near cruise speed, and shallow the bank toward 10° as the speed builds
Keep climb power until near cruise speed, and steepen the bank as she speeds up, to about 19.5°
Pull power to cruise as the nose comes down, and double the bank to about 27° for the faster speed
questions.why: To level off at cruise, hold climb power while the airplane accelerates and reduce to the cruise setting as the airspeed approaches cruise [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. At the same bank, more speed gives a slower rate of turn [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], so the bank must be varied in direct proportion to the airspeed change to hold standard rate [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. By the 15 percent rule, 90 knots needs about 13.5° and 130 knots about 19.5° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Shallowing would slow the turn further, and 27° would turn well past standard rate.

questions.q: In a retractable trainer like the IFH example, your learner slows from 120 to 95 knots in level flight with the gear and full flaps down and 25 inches set. The altimeter and VSI show level flight, but the attitude indicator shows a bar width nose-low, so she pulls it up to the horizon and climbs 150 feet. What do you teach?
options: She was right: in any configuration, level flight is the wings sitting right on the horizon bar
In the IFH example a bar width nose-low is level flight at 95 knots with the gear and flaps down
The flaps put an error into the attitude indicator, so she should hold altitude by the airspeed alone
She needed power instead: a nose-low picture in level flight always means there is too little power
questions.why: In the IFH example the attitude indicator shows about two-and-a-half bar widths nose-high in level flight at 100 knots with the gear down, and after the flaps go down with 25 inches set it shows a bar width nose-low in straight-and-level flight at 95 knots [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. Failure to interpret the attitude indicator in terms of the existing airspeed is a listed pitch error, and here the altimeter and VSI had already shown level flight [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. Knowing the power settings and trim changes for each mix of airspeed, gear and flaps reduces these interpretation problems [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

questions.q: In cloud near freezing, your learner flies a constant airspeed climb at climb power. The airspeed slowly reads higher and higher, so she raises the nose to hold climb speed. Now the stall warning sounds with the airspeed showing 15 knots above climb speed. What happened, and what does she do?
options: Pitot ram hole and drain blocked, so the airspeed acts like an altimeter: lower the nose, pitot heat on
Normal airspeed lag from momentum: hold the attitude for 6 to 9 seconds and the reading will settle
A blocked static port has frozen the altimeter: open the alternate static source and keep climbing
The stall warning must be false at that airspeed; the airspeed is primary for pitch, so she trusts it
questions.why: If the pitot ram hole and drain hole are both blocked, the airspeed indicator works like an altimeter as the airplane climbs and descends [[23:98|IFH 5-3]], showing more airspeed in a climb; visible moisture can block the pitot tube, and pitot heat use is in the AFM/POH [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. In a constant airspeed climb the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch [[23:175|IFH 7-14]], so the false reading drives the nose up. A stall warning calls for a prompt, smooth reduction of the angle of attack [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. A blocked static port does the opposite, showing less airspeed in a climb with the VSI stuck on zero [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]], and 6 to 9 seconds is the VSI's lag [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]].

questions.q: Climbing from 3,000 to 9,000 feet at climb speed in a fixed-pitch trainer, your learner sees the rate fall from 700 to 400 fpm. She raises the nose to get 700 back, and the airspeed drops 10 knots below climb speed. What do you teach?
options: Good: in any climb the VSI is primary for pitch, so she holds 700 fpm and accepts the slower airspeed
Lower the nose to the cruise attitude to build speed, then pull up again to win back the lost rate
Climb power fades with altitude: check the tachometer, advance the throttle, and pitch for climb speed
Switch to a constant rate climb: hold 700 fpm with pitch and let the airspeed settle where it will
questions.why: A normally aspirated engine loses power as altitude increases; with a fixed-pitch propeller the rpm falls, so the pilot keeps advancing the throttle to hold climb power [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. In a constant airspeed climb the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch, and the tachometer or manifold pressure gauge is the primary power instrument, monitored to make sure climb power is held [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. The rate depends on weight and atmospheric conditions [[23:208|IFH 7-47]], and under IFR a pilot unable to climb at least 500 fpm advises ATC [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]]. In a constant rate climb the airspeed is primary for power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]], so letting it decay is wrong there too.

questions.q: In a glass trainer your learner slows in level flight to her 90-knot descent speed, then reduces to the planned descent power but holds the level pitch. The airspeed sags to 80, she pushes hard, and the speed shoots to 100. What do you teach?
options: The VSI tape is primary for pitch in this descent, so she sets 500 fpm first and fixes the speed later
Bring the power back more slowly, so the airspeed stays at 90 without any change of pitch at all
This is normal airspeed tape lag; she holds the push until the speed settles, then trims it off
Lower the nose as the power comes back, then make small pitch changes, each checked on the speed tape
questions.why: On the PFD, as the airplane nears the descent airspeed, the power is reduced to a predetermined value, and the airspeed keeps decreasing below the target unless the pitch is lowered at the same time. The airspeed tape is primary for pitch: make small corrections on the attitude indicator and validate them on the airspeed tape and its trend indicator [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Changes do not give instant, stable results, so wait until one change is validated before making the next [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. The VSI tape is primary for pitch only in a constant rate descent [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Any delay in the airspeed comes from the airplane's momentum, not the instrument, which is why one small change at a time works better than a held push [[23:198|IFH 7-37]].

questions.q: In a constant rate descent planned for 500 fpm at 90 knots, your learner shows 700 fpm down and 98 knots. She reaches for the throttle. What do you coach first?
options: Power first: the airspeed is primary for power in this descent, so less power will fix both
Both point to a nose-low attitude: raise the nose slightly, then see if power is still needed
Raise the nose until the VSI reads 500, and add power so the airplane holds the faster 98 knots
Hold the attitude and wait, because the VSI needs several seconds to settle after any change
questions.why: Pitch and power corrections in a constant rate descent are coordinated as they are in climbs [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. In the IFH climb example, with the vertical speed high and the airspeed low, lower the nose slightly and watch the airspeed to decide whether power is also needed [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]; when the airspeed is low and the pitch high, pitch alone may solve it [[23:209|IFH 7-48]]. A descent rate too high with the airspeed high is the same idea as altitude low and airspeed high in level flight, where a change in pitch alone may fix both [[23:169|IFH 7-8]] [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. Failure to cross-check both airspeed and vertical speed before adjusting pitch or power is a listed error, since a change in one may correct the other [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

questions.q: Flying as your learner, the examiner is asked for a 500 fpm constant rate climb at 90 knots. He sets full power, holds 90 knots and climbs at 750 fpm. What do you say?
options: Lower the nose until the VSI shows 500 and leave full power in, since the VSI is primary for pitch
Nothing to fix: the rate depends on weight and conditions, so 750 fpm is just today's number
Wrong power for the rate: reduce toward the setting for 500 fpm and adjust pitch to keep 90 knots
Raise the nose a little, so the added drag brings the rate down to 500 fpm at full power
questions.why: At any given airspeed the power setting decides whether the airplane is level, climbing or descending [[23:169|IFH 7-8]], so 750 fpm at the right airspeed means too much power. The constant rate entry sets power to the approximate setting for the desired rate [[23:175|IFH 7-14]], and failure to learn and use proper power settings is a listed error [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. A change to any one variable needs a coordinated change in the other; more pitch raises the rate only for a moment before drag costs airspeed [[23:209|IFH 7-48]], and lowering the nose at full power would leave the airspeed high. Accepting whatever rate results is the constant airspeed method [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

questions.q: In a 500 fpm constant rate descending turn, each time your learner rolls out, the VSI falls to about 200 fpm down before she catches it. What error is this, and what is the fix?
options: Pitch not lowered as the vertical lift returns; ease the nose down as the bank comes off
Power too low for the roll-out; add power each time, since power holds the rate in this maneuver
Normal VSI lag on the roll-out; wait 6 to 9 seconds for the needle before making any correction
A roll-out that is too slow; roll out faster so the lift change is over before the VSI shows it
questions.why: As the bank decreases, the vertical component of lift increases unless the pitch is lowered, so the pitch should come down with the bank [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. Failure to adjust the pitch as the vertical lift increases on roll-out is a listed error that gives a consistent altitude gain [[23:186|IFH 7-25]], seen here as a sudden drop in the descent rate. In a constant rate descent the VSI is primary for pitch and the airspeed primary for power [[23:178|IFH 7-17]], so power is not the rate control. The roll-out rate should match the roll-in rate [[23:212|IFH 7-51]], and the change is real, not lag.

questions.q: In IMC your learner's panel looks like this. The compass, read in steady flight, shows 090, and approach says, "Turn right heading 180." What plan do you coach?
options: Level the attitude indicator's wings first, since it shows a left bank, then turn on the heading indicator
Turn by the compass with 30° of bank to get it done quickly, and roll out as the card reaches 180
Fly the turn on the attitude indicator: its flag only warns of low suction, and its picture is still good
Cover the flagged gyros, hold the calibrated turn coordinator mark for 30 seconds, then read the compass
questions.why: Flags, or an attitude indicator that disagrees with the turn coordinator and VSI, identify a failure; in Figure 11-8 the airplane is actually level at 2,000 feet, not turning left as the failed gyros suggest, and covering the failed instruments may help. The next step is usually to advise ATC [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. A timed turn uses the clock in place of the heading indicator, with the turn coordinator primary for bank: roll in as the second hand passes a cardinal point, roll out when the time is up, then check the compass allowing for deviation [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. 90° at standard rate is 30 seconds [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. Past about 18° of bank the compass is erratic [[23:106|IFH 5-11]].

questions.q: Partial panel near 40° north, your learner wants to turn from 270 to 360 by the compass quickly, so she rolls into 30° of bank. The card swings wildly, and she cannot find her roll-out point. What do you teach?
options: Keep the 30° bank: a faster turn gives the compass less time to lag, so the lead can be smaller
Use a standard-rate bank of 15° to 18°: the float tilts only to about 18°, and the lead rule assumes it
Keep the 30° bank and roll out right at 360, since a steep bank removes the northerly turning error
Keep the 30° bank and double the lead to 80°, twice the latitude, to allow for the steeper bank
questions.why: The compass float can rotate and tilt only to about 18° of bank; at steeper banks its indications are erratic and unpredictable [[23:106|IFH 5-11]]. The IFH compass turn rule is given for a bank between 15° and 18°: turning to north, the roll-out lead is about the latitude plus the normal roll-out lead [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Abrupt changes in attitude make the card move erratically and very hard to read [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. For instrument training, any turn greater than standard rate is already a steep turn [[23:183|IFH 7-22]], and no source gives a lead for steeper banks.

questions.q: Partial panel near 30° north, your learner turns right from 090 to 180 by the compass with about 15° of bank. She was taught elsewhere to stop when the card has passed south by 15° plus half the latitude, at 210. You teach starting the roll-out at 203. What do you tell her?
options: Her rule is wrong: the card leads on turns to south, so she must stop the turn before it shows 180
Her rule is right and 203 is wrong, because the IFH 7-22 numbers apply only to turns toward north
Both rules are in FAA handbooks and both go past south; use one and check it with a timed turn
Neither applies: at 15° of bank the compass shows no turning error, so she rolls out at 180
questions.why: IFH 5-13 and PHAK 8-26 let the card pass south by 15° plus half the latitude, 15 + 15 = 30 past at 30° [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]. IFH 7-22, for a 15° to 18° bank, keeps turning until the compass passes south by the latitude minus the normal roll-out lead, which gives 203 for a turn from east at 30° [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Both go past south because the card lags on southerly turns [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]. A timed turn needs no allowance for compass errors, and 90° at standard rate takes 30 seconds [[23:214|IFH 7-53]], so it is a good check on either rule.

questions.q: After a 360° steep left turn, your learner rolls out on the attitude indicator. It shows wings level, but the heading indicator keeps creeping left and the ball sits right of center. She calls it precession. What do you teach?
options: Not precession while the ball is out: right rudder to center it, stop the heading change, retrim
Precession is right: the gyro tilts in steep turns, so hold the wings level on it and wait a minute
Precession is right: reset the miniature airplane until the heading indicator stops moving
It is a slip: add left rudder toward the way the heading moves, then level the wings again
questions.why: The IFH check: if the heading changes while the attitude indicator shows level flight, the airplane is turning. If the ball is centered, the gyro has precessed; if it is not, the airplane may be slipping or skidding: center the ball with rudder, check the attitude and heading indicators, stop the heading change and retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. With the wings level and the ball displaced the airplane is skidding, and the fix is rudder on the ball's side: right ball, right rudder [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. Real precession errors after a 180° turn are small and correct themselves within a minute or so [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

questions.q: Gyros covered, your learner holds the turn coordinator well past the standard-rate mark to practice a steep turn. On each entry the altimeter unwinds fast; she yanks back, climbs, then pushes, and the turn rate wanders. What do you teach?
options: Keep the turn going and pull harder, since only more back pressure holds altitude past standard rate
Fly pitch by the VSI alone, since on round dials it shows each pitch change the moment it happens
Hold altitude with power instead: add throttle until the altimeter stops, and leave the elevator alone
Roll out and analyze, go back to shallower turns, then use small inputs: stop the needle, then return
questions.why: If pitch control is consistently late on steep turn entries, roll out at once to straight-and-level flight and analyze; practice shallower turns first, then increase the bank as the cross-check gets quicker [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. Without the attitude indicator, the rate of the altimeter needle shows the size of the pitch error, and a correction takes two distinct changes: one to stop the needle, one to return [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Rapid inputs set up an oscillation that can disorient the pilot and fix her on the altimeter, costing directional control [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]. A large, abrupt pitch change makes the VSI erratic, even reversed, and slower to settle [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]. Power in a steep turn holds the airspeed as the bank and drag increase [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]; it does not replace pitch control.

questions.q: Flying alone with little fuel, your learner slows to 105 knots, the maneuvering speed her POH gives at maximum gross weight, and rolls into a 50° instrument steep turn. What do you teach?
options: Good: maneuvering speed is the same at any weight, so 105 knots protects the airplane in this turn
Maneuvering speed drops when light, so use today's value; the stall margin shrinks as bank grows
Fly above maneuvering speed, so the higher stall speed in the bank stays far below the airspeed
Good: the load factor in a level 50° turn depends on airspeed, and at 105 knots it stays under 1.5
questions.why: Weight matters for design maneuvering speed: VA may be 100 knots when heavily loaded but only 90 knots when light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Steep turns are flown at or below VA or VO because of the higher load factors; at or below that speed the airplane stalls before exceeding its design load limit [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. The load factor for a given bank in a level turn is the same whatever the airspeed, 1.41 at 45° and 2.0 at 60°, and the stall speed rises with it, from 50 to 60 knots at 45° and 70 knots at 60°, so the margin between stall speed and maneuvering speed shrinks as the bank increases [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

questions.q: Gyros covered, your learner slows from 120 to 90 knots in a left standard-rate turn. Staring at the tachometer, she keeps adding back pressure. You see the airspeed at 70 and falling, the altimeter climbing and the turn coordinator past the left standard-rate mark. Which recovery do you coach?
options: Level the turn coordinator's wings first, then lower the nose, and then add power
Reduce power and ease back, since the airspeed is falling while the airplane climbs
Power up, push to lower the nose, then level the wings, almost at once in that order
Keep turning and shallow the bank to the 90-knot standard-rate bank to finish the slowdown
questions.why: Once an unusual attitude is noted, the immediate problem is getting back to straight-and-level flight as quickly as possible [[23:188|IFH 7-27]], so finishing the slowdown waits. Decreasing airspeed with a climbing altimeter is a nose-high attitude. The IFH sequence: increase power in proportion to the deceleration, apply forward pressure to lower the nose and prevent a stall, then level the miniature aircraft and center the ball with coordinated aileron and rudder, almost simultaneously but in that order; level pitch shows as the reversal and stabilization of the airspeed and altimeter needles [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Wings first is the nose-low order [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The cause was fixation: unnecessary gazing at the power instrument during an airspeed change is a listed error [[23:174|IFH 7-13]], and at the same bank the slowing airplane turned faster [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].

questions.q: For your Task H demonstration the examiner sets up a steep nose-high climbing turn. When you open your eyes, the stall warning is sounding and the airframe is buffeting. What do you do first, and why?
options: Push to reduce the angle of attack until the warning stops, then roll level and add power
Full power first, then push, then roll: the IFH nose-high sequence for a falling airspeed
Roll the wings level first so the lift points up, then push and add power together
Add full power and hold the attitude, since power alone flies the airplane out of a stall
questions.why: Once the stall warning or buffet is there, fly the stall recovery: reduce the angle of attack first, until the impending stall indications are gone, and do not be tempted to control the bank before that; then roll wings level and add power as needed. Adding power reduces the altitude loss but does not eliminate a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. The IFH also answers a stall warning by smoothly reducing the angle of attack [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Its nose-high order, power, then pitch, then bank, is for an airspeed decreasing toward a stall [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

questions.q: In IMC your learner levels off abruptly from a 1,000 fpm climb. She says she feels she is tumbling backward and keeps pushing. Now the airspeed is rising, the altimeter unwinding and the turn coordinator showing a right turn. What do you coach now, and for next time?
options: Add power and pull firmly, because the tumbling feeling means the nose is high, whatever the panel says
Raise the nose first, then level the wings, then reduce power, which is the fastest way out of a dive
Hold the present attitude until the feeling passes, then level off again on the attitude indicator
Power back, wings level on the turn coordinator, then smooth back pressure; next time a 100-foot lead
questions.why: An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can create the inversion illusion of tumbling backward, and the disoriented pilot may push abruptly nose-low [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Rising airspeed and a falling altimeter mean nose-low: reduce power, level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder by the turn coordinator, then raise the nose with smooth back pressure; the instinctive reaction is to pull first [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Next time, lead the level-off by 10 percent of the vertical speed, 100 feet at 1,000 fpm, with smooth, steady forward pressure [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

questions.q: Your glass learner looks up from a chart and sees this PFD during a simulated AHRS failure, in an airplane equipped like the IFH example. How does she know her attitude, and what does she use to level the wings?
options: She waits for the red chevrons, which still point back to the horizon after the AHRS has failed
Altitude and VSI tapes show nose-high; push, and level wings on the standby attitude indicator
The slip/skid indicator and the standby turn coordinator still show the bank, so she levels on those
The compass shows a steady heading, so the wings must be level and only the nose needs to come down
questions.why: An AHRS failure removes all unusual attitude protection and all attitude and heading indications on the PFD. In Figure 7-73 the altimeter and VSI tape are the only clear signs of the nose-high attitude, the slip/skid indicator is gone, no standby turn coordinator is installed, and the magnetic compass is not as useful as a turn coordinator or slip/skid indicator [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. The standby instruments, an analog airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass, are what remain [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. In a nose-high attitude, forward elevator pressure lowers the nose, with power added as needed for a decreasing airspeed [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

questions.q: Gyros covered, your learner recovers from a nose-low spiral: power back, wings level on the turn coordinator, then a firm pull. She keeps pulling until the VSI reads zero and ends up nose-high, with the airspeed dropping and the altimeter climbing. What do you teach?
options: She should pull harder and sooner, so that the VSI reaches zero before the airspeed can build up
She should read pitch from the turn coordinator, whose miniature airplane also shows the nose attitude
The VSI lags after a big pull; ease off as the airspeed and altimeter needles slow, stop when they stop
That is normal: every nose-low recovery ends a little nose-high, so she simply waits for it to settle
questions.why: After the first control inputs, keep a fast cross-check for overcontrolling, since the initial pressures may be large. As the altimeter and airspeed needles slow, the attitude is approaching level; when they stop and reverse, the airplane is passing through level [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. A large, abrupt pitch change makes the VSI needle erratic, can reverse it and adds lag [[23:166|IFH 7-5]], so waiting for zero on the VSI after a firm pull invites the overshoot. A turn coordinator does not sense pitch; some are even marked NO PITCH INFORMATION [[23:117|IFH 5-22]].
